title: Cloudflare debuts Clairic, a System One-class extraction model it says processes unstructured data faster, more cheaply, and more accurately than normal LLMs
excerpt: Cloudflare debuts Clairic, a System One-class extraction model it says processes unstructured data faster, more cheaply, and more accurately than normal LLMs
title_en: Cloudflare debuts Clairic, a System One-class extraction model it says processes unstructured data faster, more cheaply, and more accurately than normal LLMs
excerpt_en: Cloudflare debuts Clairic, a System One-class extraction model it says processes unstructured data faster, more cheaply, and more accurately than normal LLMs
content_en:
# Introducing Clairic, a new System One class of extraction models

Today, we're announcing a preview of a new class of System One-style models: extraction models. Our first one, Clairic, is available hosted on Workers AI as `@cf/cloudflare/clairic.`We intend to release the model open-weights soon. Clairic is an extraction model that is able to extract, compute, estimate, and forecast values from unstructured inputs — all at a significantly higher accuracy, faster latency, and cheaper cost than traditional LLMs.

## Context

When System One models were announced by TypeSafe a month ago, it took the industry by storm. As referenced by <u>TypeSafe in their blog</u> and defined by Daniel Kahneman’s book *Thinking, Fast and Slow*, a System One model should be fast and precise, which contrasts a System Two model that is capable of deliberate reasoning (like LLMs). With this, TypeSafe introduced Jev — a model that is purpose-fit for a specific use case, and priced accessibly given its niche domain. It excelled where LLMs failed, helping users make decisions based on probabilities and well-typed outputs. The introduction of Jev prompted people to start thinking about a new class of models that were not LLMs and how to integrate them into their workflows.

We were inspired by the concept of System One models and started thinking about other tasks where LLMs are inefficient. There are many structured-output calls going to frontier LLMs today with the same shapes again and again: *What's the invoice total? When was this delivered? How many days late is it? What will this repair cost? What will traffic look like over the next 24 hours?* None of these have answers you can list out in advance, which is needed for a decision model to give probabilities against. That led us to the class of models we're introducing today: System One extraction models.

## Introducing System One extraction models

Until now, every System One model has been a decision model: Jev and <u>Clef</u> take an input state and a list of questions and give probabilities against the inputs and your listed questions. <u>Clairic</u> is the first model in a new class: System One extraction models. It is still fast, typed, and cheap, but it answers with **values** directly extracted from the input, computed from it, or predicted beyond it.

Most model tasks ask for one of three kinds of output: a number, a choice from a fixed set, or open-ended text. Clairic handles the first, returning numbers with an 80% range, and also pulls typed values like names, dates and lists out of the input. Clef handles the second: it picks among options and returns a probability for each. LLMs handle the third. We call Clairic and Clef System One models because they answer in a single pass, without reasoning or generating tokens. They charge only for input and typically respond in under a second, while an LLM that reasons through the same step takes several seconds.

An extraction model can return:

- **Extracted values:** Text copied from the input, such as a name, an order ID or a description. Each one comes back as a span with its character offsets and a confidence score.
- Including, **computed values:** Numbers, dates, times, datetimes, durations and lists, read from the input or worked out from it. They follow the rules of their type (for example, two decimals for cents) and come with a confidence score.
- **Estimated values:** Values the input doesn't state but gives evidence for. Each one comes back as a distribution inside the bounds you declare, on the grid you specify, with a median and an 80% interval.
- **Forecasted values:** Future values of a series, one estimate per step ahead, each with its own 80% interval.

And because it generates no tokens, it can't produce a mistyped answer or “hallucinate” in the same way as an LLM (though it can, of course, make mistakes). Outputs are a value of the type you asked for, or null when the model fails to find an answer in the input. It also comes with confidence scores against the outputs to help you evaluate if it is appropriate to trust the model or to take a second look.

Here’s how extraction models fit into the landscape of System One and System Two models:

Together, these models can work together in unison to help you get closer to parsing through real-world data, making decisions on inputs, and then taking actions. Extraction models turn raw input into typed values, decision models turn values into decisions, and LLMs turn decisions into words.

## How a request works

Clairic is designed differently than an LLM. Similar to a decision model, it only processes input tokens with a single forward pass, and thus has no charge for output tokens. It is much faster, cheaper, and more accurate than an LLM for certain use cases.

A request is a `state` (the text to read, plus up to four optional images) and a map of typed `fields`. You name each field, give it a type and optional plain-language `instructions`, and get back one typed answer per field, all from one parallel pass. There is no reasoning and no output tokens – everything computes in a single forward pass, which means it is both fast and cheap.

Every scalar answer comes with `p_null` (the probability that the value isn’t in the inputs) and `confidence`. Every `estimate` answer comes with a median and an 80% interval (`p10` to `p90`), plus all 99 percentiles on request. There's no limit on the number of fields: if they don't fit beside the input in one pass, the server splits them into parallel passes that each see the whole input, then merges the answers.

Here are some examples to illustrate the model’s features. Of course, using these features in a workflow would require appropriate inputs.

## An example: Extracting values

Extraction is probably the most common job handed to LLMs today: "return the invoice number, vendor and due date as JSON." It works most of the time, but the failure modes are hard to catch. The output may not be valid JSON, a digit can be misread as it's generated, and once a text excerpt comes back, there's no way to trace it to where it appeared in the source. Most people build extraction pipelines to combat this, with multiple layers of parsing, schema validation, retries and spot checks. On top of that, you pay for reasoning and output tokens on every field of every document.

Clairic operates differently; it doesn’t generate text answers. Instead, you get:

- **Values** extracted from your input, so an answer is grounded.
- **Computed values**, so it can parse through unstructured data without pre-sanitizing it.
- **Character offset spans**, so you can reference where in the input the data was.
- **Confidence labels**, so you can determine which values need a second look.
- **A strongly typed output**, so numbers and dates are formed under the rules of their type (e.g., a cents field has two decimals).
- **Handling for null values**, where a missing field returns with `null` as an answer (along with an estimated probability of null and a guess).
- **Cheaper and faster answers**, because every field is answered in the same parallel pass. So asking for thirty fields costs about the same as asking for three.

Let’s walk through an example to illustrate the ways Clairic can extract values from unstructured data and make estimates. Take a customer support email:

*Hi, order A-88412 arrived on Sept 28, 2026 with a cracked screen and a dented corner. I paid $649.00 plus $52.10 tax. It's now Oct 9, 2026 and I'd like this fixed or refunded. Thanks, Dana*

From a Worker, you would make a request to Clairic to process this data:

```
const { answers } = await env.AI.run("@cf/cloudflare/clairic", {
  state: email,
  fields: {
    order_id:            { type: "text", instructions: "Order number" },
    delivered_on:        { type: "date", instructions: "Delivery date" },
    amount_paid:         { type: "number", decimals: 2, unit: "USD", instructions: "Total paid including tax" },
    da

title: Advancing Coding in Low-Resource Programming Languages
excerpt: Learn how OpenAI is improving ChatGPT across low-resource programming languages, with new evaluations for software engineering, SQLite, and COBOL migration.
title_en: Advancing Coding in Low-Resource Programming Languages
excerpt_en: Learn how OpenAI is improving ChatGPT across low-resource programming languages, with new evaluations for software engineering, SQLite, and COBOL migration.
content_en:
# Advancing coding in low‑resource programming languages

Our latest model advances bring stronger capabilities for building and migrating software in low-resource programming languages such as COBOL, Fortran, and Visual Basic. These languages have less code and documentation available for models to learn from than languages like Python and JavaScript, yet support critical infrastructure and essential services around the world. COBOL supports(opens in a new window) more than 40% of online banking systems, 80% of in-person credit card transactions and 95% of ATM transactions, while Fortran is used in weather forecasting(opens in a new window) and nuclear reactor safety analysis(opens in a new window). Improving AI’s ability to work in these languages could help teams maintain and modernize the software that essential services depend on.

This work is guided by feedback from developers and enterprise customers who have told us that coding models often struggle with these languages. Maintaining and modernizing this software can be difficult: documentation may be incomplete, original developers may have left the company, and important business rules may only exist in code. Whether teams are fixing bugs or migrating to another language, they need to preserve the behavior their systems depend on.

To measure progress, we developed two evaluations. MultiLangBench tests whether a model can build a SQLite-compatible database engine from scratch across 20 different programming languages. Our COBOL migration evaluation tests whether a model can migrate existing programs to another language while preserving their behavior. Together, they test two complementary skills: building new software and preserving what existing software does.

Our latest models show substantial improvements across both evaluations, delivering much higher accuracy at lower cost.

On MultiLangBench, GPT‑6 Astra achieves an average test pass rate of 87.4% across 20 programming languages, up from 26.8% for GPT‑5.6 Sol, with improvements in every language tested. GPT‑6 Luna also outperforms GPT‑5.6 Sol, reaching 40.3% at approximately 78% lower estimated API cost.

On our COBOL migration evaluation, GPT‑6.1 Sol achieves 86.6% accuracy at low reasoning effort, compared with just 5.4% for GPT‑5.6 Sol, while costing 39% less. At higher reasoning effort, accuracy reaches 97.9%, nearly saturating the evaluation.

Together, these results show that our models are becoming significantly better at working with a wide range of programming languages, while also becoming more cost-efficient.

MultiLangBench asks a model to build a SQLite-compatible database engine in a specified programming language. The model must organize a codebase, manage state, handle errors, and add new features while preserving existing functionality.

To compare implementations across languages, we use database files as a shared interface. The candidate program receives an initial database and a SQL query, then produces a modified database. We use the reference SQLite implementation to check whether the resulting database has the expected contents. This lets us apply the same tests regardless of the language used to build the engine.

We adapted tests from SQLite’s existing test suite to this format. The evaluation measures how much working functionality a model can build over an extended coding session, reporting both test pass rate and API cost.

At maximum reasoning effort, GPT‑6 Astra achieves an average test pass rate of 87.4% across the 20 languages, up from 26.8% for GPT‑5.6 Sol. Improvements extend to every language tested, including COBOL (10.9% to 72.1%), OCaml (25.6% to 85.8%), Fortran (21.4% to 83.5%), and Visual Basic (27.5% to 89.4%). Astra scores above 83% in 19 of the 20 languages, with COBOL remaining the hardest at 72%.

GPT‑6 Luna offers a lower-cost option that also improves on GPT‑5.6 Sol in every language tested. At maximum reasoning effort, it reaches an average test pass rate of 40.3%. Gains include COBOL (10.9% to 17.1%), OCaml (25.6% to 34.1%), Fortran (21.4% to 31.4%), and Visual Basic (27.5% to 41.6%). These improvements come at an estimated average API cost of $0.77 per sample, compared with $3.48 for GPT‑5.6 Sol, approximately 78% lower.

We are releasing the MultiLangBench evaluation setup and test suite on GitHub(opens in a new window), along with results for each language. Developers can inspect what the evaluation tests, review performance in the languages they use, and identify gaps that matter for their own work.

Our second evaluation asks models to migrate COBOL programs to C++, Java, Kotlin, Python, or Rust while preserving what each program does.

Successful migration requires understanding both the program’s business logic and COBOL’s specific language behavior. COBOL programs often process financial transactions and business records, where details such as rounding rules and missing-record handling reflect business requirements. For example, COBOL’s fixed-point arithmetic discards excess decimal digits unless rounding is explicitly requested. A rewrite that rounds those values instead can run without errors while producing different financial results.

To test whether these behaviors are preserved, we evaluate our models on hidden tests that require byte-for-byte parity on observable outputs. A migration is considered successful only if all tests pass. Behavior-preserving capabilities like these are useful for teams maintaining and modernizing older systems, though applying it to production software still requires expert review and testing against the system’s business rules and dependencies.

On this evaluation, GPT‑6.1 Sol achieves 86.6% accuracy at low reasoning effort, compared with GPT‑5.6 Sol’s 5.4% at the same setting at just 61% of the API cost. At higher reasoning effort, accuracy reaches 97.9%, bringing the evaluation close to saturation. These evaluation results demonstrate progress toward more accurate, affordable code migration for teams modernizing the software their businesses depend on.

These evaluations, alongside direct feedback from developers and enterprise customers, help us see where our models are improving and where they still fall short.

Our goal is to help models apply software engineering skills across more languages: understanding unfamiliar repositories, planning changes, using build tools, running tests, and debugging failures.

You can try our latest models through the API on coding tasks in the languages your team uses. Your feedback on what works, where the models struggle, and which languages or workflows we should focus on next helps shape how we train and evaluate models to better support the software you depend on.

content_en:
### MiniMax launches M3.1 Flash model, says it cuts AI agent costs by 70%

Chinese artificial intelligence developer MiniMax Group Inc. today released M3.1 Flash, a faster and cheaper update to the M3 large language model it launched in June.

The release takes aim at the cost of running AI agents, which often need dozens of model calls to finish a single job. MiniMax said Flash represents its “ongoing exploration of the balance between efficiency and capability.” Agentic tasks cost 70% less to run than on its previous model, the company said, and inference is close to three times as fast, with output at everyday peak topping 200 tokens per second.

Size has barely changed from M3. MiniMax’s developer guide for the preview release lists 428 billion parameters in all, and the launch post credits the extra speed to more aggressive sparsity at inference time. Reasoning stays on for every request, with developers choosing one of five effort levels from Low to Max. The model accepts text, image and video input, and prompts can run to 1 million tokens.

In MiniMax’s own testing, M3.1 Flash scored 61.7 on OSWorld V2, which tests how well a model can operate a computer, and the company said no Chinese model has done better. BankerToolBench, a banking workflow test, gave it 76.2.

For security work, MiniMax pointed to an 82% score on CyberGym. University of California, Berkeley researchers built that benchmark to test whether AI agents can reproduce real software vulnerabilities, and the company listed code auditing, penetration testing and malware analysis among the jobs M3.1 Flash can take on.

At a flat 15 cents per million input tokens, M3.1 Flash lines up directly against the V4.1-Flash model from Hangzhou DeepSeek Artificial Intelligence Basic Technology Research Co. Ltd., which charges the same rate off-peak. DeepSeek said over the weekend that its updated V4.1-Flash resolved 77% of tasks on the DeepSWE v1.1 software engineering test. M3.1 Flash managed 73.7%, and neither result has been checked independently.

MiniMax, which has traded in Hong Kong since a $619 million initial public offering in January, saw its shares fall after the original V4.1-Flash launched in September, Bloomberg reported.

The launch also settles who was behind Space Bunny, an anonymous model that turned up on OpenRouter Inc.’s model routing service in late September. Community testers soon linked it to MiniMax by probing its tokenizer, and the company confirmed today that Space Bunny was an early M3.1 Flash build. More than 200 trillion tokens went through it while its maker stayed unnamed, according to the launch post.

M3.1 Flash is available now through the MiniMax API, the company’s M Plan subscription and its MiniMax Code desktop app. Output costs 60 cents per million tokens and cached input 1.5 cents. The company said it will release the Flash weights later, and a more capable Pro model is also coming.

content_en:
### Nvidia, Dell back $200M round for AI model developer doubleAI

Artificial intelligence developer doubleAI today announced that it has raised $200 million in funding.

Lightspeed and Bessemer co-led the Series A round. They were joined by Nvidia Corp., Dell Technologies Inc. and several others. CTech reported that the investment values doubleAI at more than $1 billion.

Tel Aviv-based doubleAI, officially AA-I Technologies Ltd., has created an AI model called Maxwell that can automatically make software code more efficient. It also lends itself to a variety of other tasks. Maxwell broke a long-standing chess challenge earlier this month, while a doubleAI-developed agent made a new mathematical discovery around the same time.

Nvidia offers an open-source library called cuGraph that enables customers to harness its graphics cards for graph analytics. That’s a data science approach used in fields such as supply chain management. In March, doubleAI revealed that Maxwell had rewritten cuGraph to lower its hardware usage. The company says that the model sped up 55% of the algorithms in the library by a factor of two or more.

Maxwell went on to create an optimized version of pandas, a popular open-source data science toolkit. The AI improved the library’s performance on PDS-H, a query speed benchmark, by a factor of 38. A more recent project saw doubleAI use Maxwell to double the video generation speed of a world model called LTX-2.5.

The company plans to sell the model to enterprises interested in lowering their AI workloads’ hardware usage. According to doubleAI, Maxwell finds optimization opportunities by analyzing how a program interacts with the data that it processes and the underlying chips. The model supports both graphics processing units and central processing units.

Processors don’t run applications’ source code directly. Instead, they run a version of the source code called a binary. It’s a machine-generated translation that represents a program as a series of simple computing operations.

When developers find a way to make an application more efficient, they usually implement the optimization by modifying the program’s source code. Maxwell, by contrast, applies optimizations to a program’s binary. That removes the need for developers to manually make source code changes. Furthermore, doubleAI’s approach makes it possible to modify applications while they’re running in production.

The company’s technology also lends itself to other use cases. Earlier this month, doubleAI used an internal AI agent to make a new discovery about graphs, mathematical structures with an important role in software development. The agent paired its proof with a Lean file, a code snippet that makes it relatively simple to verify the finding.

In conjunction with today’s funding announcement, doubleAI revealed that Maxwell recently broke a nearly 50-year chess record. The model found a chess position, or arrangement of chess pieces, in which 63 moves give check. The previous record was 60 moves.

The Wall Street Journal reported that doubleAI will use half its funding round to buy 1,000 of Nvidia’s B300 Blackwell graphics cards. The chips should make it easier for the company to compete with OpenAI Group PBC and Anthropic PBC, whose latest AI models are also capable of automating research tasks.

A few days ago, the ChatGPT developer released 722 AI-generated math papers. A month earlier, an Anthropic model created a computer-verifiable version of a famous mathematical proof. The file comprises 13 million lines of code that would have taken a team of human mathematicians several years to write.

title: Microsoft says AI agents are like insider threats as ‘frontier models can’t be trusted’
excerpt: Microsoft wants enterprises to closely watch the agents employees use with systems not controlled by AI labs like OpenAI and Anthropic.
title_en: Microsoft says AI agents are like insider threats as ‘frontier models can’t be trusted’
excerpt_en: Microsoft wants enterprises to closely watch the agents employees use with systems not controlled by AI labs like OpenAI and Anthropic.
content_en:
Microsoft on Monday introduced new security features designed to protect enterprises from the growing threat of AI agents. The launch comes at Microsoft continues to warn enterprises about the dangers of AI and agents.

Perhaps the most notable addition is Guardian Agents, a new feature intended to monitor the AI agents a company uses. Guardian Agents is part of Project Perception, a product introduced in June.

Project Perception was Microsoft’s answer to powerful hacking models like Anthropic’s Mythos and Fable and OpenAI’s security vulnerability scanning system Daybreak. Project Perception originally launched three classes of agents: a “red team” that acted like hackers and attacked, a “blue team” that detected the red team and assessed the vulnerabilities they found, and a “green team” tasked with fixing them.

The product was designed around the assumption that AI hackers would come from outside the company. But lately, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella has been warning that the AI enemy may be the very agents enterprises have deployed and are paying for, much like a rogue human employee, otherwise known as an “insider threat.”

Earlier this month, in his private blog, Nadella warned that it’s time to stop trusting AI model providers, even if they offer assurances of safety and security with their agentic products. He wants enterprises to implement separate systems, not controlled by the AI labs, to watch and control the agents that those AI labs’ products launch.

“We are deploying these complex agentic systems and models, with access to our most sensitive data and giving them the ability to take mission-critical actions on our behalf!” he wrote. “We simply can’t outsource responsibility for what intelligence does on our behalf. A model provider’s assurances do not relieve us of that responsibility. … In other words, we need to separate the supply of intelligence from the authority over it.”

When announcing Guardian Agents, Microsoft’s security business chief Hayete Gallot was even more straightforward.

“Unfortunately, frontier models, regardless of their origin, cannot be trusted,” she wrote, adding that this isn’t because they are malicious or easily hacked, but because they are unpredictable. They have been trained to achieve tasks, not follow “organizational norms or judgment.”

On top of that, they are often given the keys to the kingdom, with access to data and tools that could do serious harm.

Microsoft’s solution is both surprising and self-serving. The surprising side is that Microsoft is famously close to OpenAI and Anthropic, having invested in both. OpenAI is also one of its biggest cloud customers, and Microsoft has its own AI lab developing models. So, Microsoft is sowing distrust against some of its own business interests.

The self-serving side is that Microsoft wants enterprises to buy agent security products from it, the cloud provider, rather than from Anthropic and OpenAI. But conflicting interests aside, its logic is sound. The software that monitors agent behavior should be separate from the suppliers of agents, just as auditors should be independent of the organizations they audit.

Or as Nadella puts it: “We need to separate the supply of intelligence from the authority over it.”

Microsoft is now seizing that business opportunity in a variety of ways. In addition to Guardian Agents, it has added an agent detection feature to its Microsoft Defender product that can find up to 60 types of agents that employees bring into the workplace, including Claude Code, Codex, and OpenClaw. It has also added features that limit agents’ access to data and systems, and dynamically adjust their agent permissions based on the task. That includes requiring human approval if an agent appears to be making risky decisions.

This idea of agents as untrustworthy insiders is taking hold across the broader industry, too.

Microsoft was an inaugural member of Nvidia’s new Open Agent Safety Platform, which garnered the support of more than 100 other tech companies. The platform isolates agents in secure environments and can monitor and stop behavior through hardware, functioning something like a kill switch. This follows Microsoft’s announcement of the new Surface Laptop Ultra PCs built for agents, which run on Nvidia chips and have agent security and controls baked in.

title: Amazon is taking its biggest shot at Nvidia yet with new TorchNeuron dev tool
excerpt: Amazon wants to break Nvidia’s hold on PyTorch, the free toolkit used to build most AI apps, so that more developers run their apps on alternative chips like its own.
title_en: Amazon is taking its biggest shot at Nvidia yet with new TorchNeuron dev tool
excerpt_en: Amazon wants to break Nvidia’s hold on PyTorch, the free toolkit used to build most AI apps, so that more developers run their apps on alternative chips like its own.
content_en:
On Monday, Amazon Web Services released a tool called TorchNeuron that lets AI startups easily move their AI apps onto Amazon’s AI chip, Trainium. In doing so, Amazon is also taking a direct stab at the software advantage that has helped Nvidia become the default hardware choice for AI apps and spurred its rise as AI hardware provider of choice.

TorchNeuron works with PyTorch, a free, open source toolkit that developers use to build, train, and run AI models. It lets AI apps written with PyTorch run on Trainium by changing just one line of configuration, according to Amazon — no code rewrite required.

Amazon says about 85% of AI apps are written with PyTorch. Facebook originally developed it, but since 2022, it has been part of the Linux Foundation, which maintains open source projects. Nvidia has spent years ensuring its CUDA software — the software infrastructure that allows apps to run on Nvidia GPUs and its other hardware — seamlessly supports AI apps written with PyTorch. As a result, Nvidia’s hardware is now deeply embedded in the toolkit, essentially by default.

TorchNeuron is adapted from PyTorch, so developers who know PyTorch already know how to use it. Amazon isn’t the first company to attempt to easily bring their chips to the platform. PyTorch users can also port their apps to AMD GPUs or even Apple’s chips with a simple configuration change.

However, Amazon argues that porting to Trainium is not only easy, but it also gives AI startups access to Amazon’s entire cloud. Unsurprisingly, AWS claims that this is a better choice for startups than using neoclouds, many of which are tied to Nvidia and its hardware, like CoreWeave, Nebius, and Firmus.

“You’re building on AWS. You’re not betting on a single-purpose compute provider and scrambling to build everything else around it,” Colin Brace, VP of Technology Software at AWS Annapurna Labs (the unit that makes Amazon’s custom chips), told TechCrunch via email. “On AWS,” he continued, “the infrastructure to go from prototype to production is already there, allowing a founder to move fast and scale when they need to.”

AWS says that because the same chip both handles training (teaching the AI model) and inference (putting the finished model to work, as when it answers a user’s question), and is tightly integrated with the cloud infrastructure that startups need, its cloud will save them money, even if AWS doesn’t offer the cheapest per-token price.

“Trainium’s value is price-performance plus the fact that it’s one platform for both training and inference, which improves the economics across a full workload,” Brace said. “Look at Deepgram — they moved to Trainium using native PyTorch support and they’re processing 70% more audio per dollar at production-grade accuracy.” Deepgram is an AI voice app provider, a competitor to ElevenLabs.

But Amazon isn’t content to just give PyTorch app developers an easy option to move to its cloud.

Amazon also says it is pushing PyTorch to be less automatically centered on Nvidia, and it will contribute the code to do that to the main PyTorch project. In the blog post announcing the new tool, the company wrote:

Amazon’s approach extends beyond its own hardware. The company is contributing changes upstream to PyTorch itself, working with the PyTorch community to remove code that ties the framework to specific chips. The goal is to make PyTorch more hardware-agnostic for the entire developer community, not just Trainium users.


While such a tactic is undoubtedly good for those who are selling hardware and cloud services that compete with Nvidia, one of the points of PyTorch is to hide all the pesky difficulties of getting AI code to run on hardware. We’ll have to wait and see if pushing Nvidia out that far gives developers more choice and more affordable options, as Amazon promises, or just more configuration headaches.

Either way, if Amazon succeeds in deeply uncoupling PyTorch from Nvidia, this could have much bigger ramifications for the GPU giant than simply dealing with chip competitors. As Brace said: “The real story is removing the lock-in that kept developers from having a real choice at all.”

title: Embedded AI evaluators won’t be an easy solution, Hugging Face’s policy chief says

title_en: Embedded AI evaluators won’t be an easy solution, Hugging Face’s policy chief says
excerpt_en: AI labs have staked their reputations on model benchmarking — the supposedly neutral and accurate system of evaluations that are designed to measure whether one AI product is better than another. However, the methods behind these evaluations are complicated and still maturing, said Irene Solaiman, Hugging Face’s chief policy officer, during a discussion at TechCrunch […]
content_en:
AI labs have staked their reputations on model benchmarking — the supposedly neutral and accurate system of evaluations that are designed to measure whether one AI product is better than another.

However, the methods behind these evaluations are complicated and still maturing, said Irene Solaiman, Hugging Face’s chief policy officer, during a discussion at TechCrunch Disrupt last week. Testing needs to come together into a more consistent science if the industry is to rely on them in the future.

With that in mind, can we trust the current tests that are being released?

“Trust is such a weighted term,” said Solaiman. “In terms of whether we can trust results, one big part \[of that\] is can you reproduce the results of an evaluation? Do you have the level of access that you need to the model itself — this is where open weights come in in a big way,” she added.

Reproducibility in model evaluations has long remained one of the stickier aspects of benchmarking — and remains a topic of significant debate in the industry.

Outside of an individual test’s validity, there’s also the added question of how that test compares to other evaluations.

“They are an evolving science — where we don’t know how to meaningfully compare them to each other,” Solaiman said.

“They start to get ineffective relatively quickly, and we don’t have as much of a thriving ecosystem as we need,” she added. “There’s this hunger for an embedded evaluator ecosystem now, but the qualifications that determine who is an effective evaluator across what tasks need a lot more standardization.”

The idea of embedded evaluators — in which supposedly “neutral” third-party observers are placed inside AI organizations — has been popularized over the last several months, as AI labs grapple with a rash of safety incidents that have spurred concerns over the potential harms of their technology. Hugging Face was famously the target of one of those incidents.

Instead of active government regulation to identify and mitigate model safety concerns, labs have pushed for the third-party solution. However, doubts remain over how neutral or effective those evaluators will actually be. Anthropic’s decision to hire Accenture as its first evaluator spurred a good amount of backlash, with some critics mocking the idea that the consulting firm was qualified to do the task at hand.

Evaluations are now moving from merely a test of the model itself to a test of the entire system around the model — including the harness and agent. The harness — or the tool the user is using to access the model — specifically, has a lot to do with a model’s performance, and a weaker model with a better harness could easily out perform a frontier model, Soleiman shared.

“Agentic evals are really hard and really expensive,” said Solaiman. “We have just more evaluations for models. … We don’t have as many evaluations for harnesses, and we are developing better evaluations for the holistic agent — because that’s what a lot of folks are getting value out of,” she added.

In other words: the evaluation space is a bit of a free-for-all at the moment, and if benchmarking is going to continue to be seen as a useful tool for industry leaders, a more uniform, industry-wide approach — where everyone is on the same page — may be necessary.

content_en:
CoreWeave had a bad week last week. Its bonds slipped into distressed territory by a common definition — when investors demand 1,000 basis points more in yield than they’d get from government bonds. Last Tuesady Chamath “SPAC King” Palihapitiya noticed the distressed debt, and also asked whether the AI buildout was a private credit bubble. Its shares are down more than 20 percent since Tuesday’s close, which is kind of a lot! There even seemed to be some collateral damage in the market on other AI companies, too.

# CoreWeave’s debt is becoming the whole AI industry’s problem

Does anyone else hear that ticking sound?

Does anyone else hear that ticking sound?

Now, I have *also* asked if the AI industry is a bubble, but when the SPAC King echoes concerns held by a lady whose ongoing question about AI is “How are we planning on affording this, champs?”, that’s a very different signal. When I say “yikes,” it’s one thing. When Elon Musk says it, that’s something else.

When you talk about wanting to tap into the enormous sums of money that insurers have, that’s the kind of thing that makes investors afraid that CoreWeave is going to borrow even more

To make things worse for CoreWeave, Brannin McBee, one of the company’s cofounders, told the *Financial Times* — *also* last week, on the same day as Palihapitiya’s post — that the company wants to have its debt be investment-grade, rather than junk, so that it can borrow from insurers, as their capital is, in his words, “unlimited.” This is not entirely unreasonable — earlier this year, CoreWeave secured its first investment-grade chip loan. But when you talk about wanting to tap into the enormous sums of money that insurers have, that’s the kind of thing that makes investors afraid that CoreWeave — already a massive debtor — is going to borrow even more.

“The problem is not that credit profiles have changed in the last year, it’s that we’ve got another year and a half of supply coming,” *Bloomberg* quoted John Yovanovic, co-head of leveraged finance at MetLife Investment Management, as saying.

I have seen people suggest that this means the AI bubble is bursting. I am not so sure. A plunging stock price is not necessarily financial doom. Stocks are an expression of confidence in a company’s future, not a reflection of day-to-day business. But CoreWeave has a lot of very expensive debt, and if that debt gets more expensive, that makes it even harder for CoreWeave to turn a profit.

CoreWeave is the poster child for AI debt, and as of its second quarter earnings, owed more than $35 billion. That’s partly because it pioneered GPUs as collateral for loans, and partly because CoreWeave doesn’t have a real business beyond selling compute, a business on which it does not make money — the company lost more than a billion dollars in the first half of the year.

The anxieties investors have around CoreWeave are, in fact, present for all neoclouds

So why am I not ready to do a victory lap on this? After all, I have suggested that this business is long-term unsustainable. The answer is “remaining performance obligations” from its customers — $103.7 billion of them as of the second quarter. About 40 percent of that money is due to CoreWeave in 2028, and the companies who’ve agreed to these contracts can’t cancel them except under some very limited circumstances. Its biggest customers are Microsoft, OpenAI, and what is probably Nvidia, though CoreWeave doesn’t disclose who its third-biggest customer is. Those three generated almost three-quarters of the company’s second quarter revenue.

Microsoft and Nvidia are probably good for the money — at least, as long as it benefits them to be good for the money. (I suspect they realize that if CoreWeave goes belly-up, there will be plenty of collateral damage in the market, so they are unlikely to push the company over the edge themselves.) OpenAI is shakier, but unless OpenAI is in significantly more financial distress than we all realize, CoreWeave is probably fine for a while. As long as it can continue to pay off its debt, the music keeps going. Only when the AI boom falters are we going to find out if it’s actually a viable business.

Still, the angst around CoreWeave has made things shaky for other companies that have taken out significant debt in the AI buildout — Oracle’s shares, for instance, which have fallen almost 10 percent in the same timeframe. There’s been a sell-off in Oracle bonds, too. The anxieties investors have around CoreWeave are, in fact, present for all neoclouds. It’s just not clear the bare-metal business is a good one.

Anyway, some people are buying the dip.
